vapid

VAP-id · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Vapid is lacking excitement, flavor, or real substance.

She scrolled past yet another vapid celebrity post promising life-changing wisdom in a single hollow sentence.

Example

The influencer's 'motivational' post -- 'good vibes only, believe in yourself' -- was so vapid that not a single follower could say what it actually meant.

Sounding upbeat while saying essentially nothing of substance is exactly the hollow emptiness vapid describes.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

lifeless: Lifeless describes delivery with all the energy drained out -- a monotone reading, a flat, mechanical performance. It says nothing about the ideas, which may be excellent. Vapid is the opposite complaint: the delivery can sparkle and shout, yet there is no real substance underneath.

frivolous: Frivolous criticizes a lack of seriousness -- joking through a solemn meeting, fussing over trifles while real work waits. A frivolous remark treats a serious matter lightly; a vapid one can sound perfectly earnest and serious yet contain no real substance at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

engaging: interesting and able to hold attention

stimulating: exciting the mind; thought-provoking

Where it sits · how empty the content is — bland → vapid → insipid

bland vs. vapid: Bland is milder than vapid: a bland speech plays it safe and unexciting but can still carry real information, while a vapid one offers nothing solid at all beneath its pleasant surface.

insipid vs. vapid: Insipid goes further than vapid: a vapid answer is merely empty of real substance, while an insipid one is so flat and watery that it actively wears the listener down, like plain water where soup was promised.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — vap-

root — vap-: flat, having lost its spirit (Latin vapidus, likely related to vapor)

suffix — -id

suffix — -id: having the quality of (as in vivid) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Vapid comes from Latin vapidus, 'flat, having lost its spirit' -- likely related to vapor -- with -id meaning 'having the quality of,' as in vivid. Originally used for wine gone stale, vapid still describes anything whose lively essence has evaporated.

Use the root in a new word: vapor

Use the root in a new word: vapor: Thin vapor rose off the lake's surface in the cold morning air.

Word Choice

Vapid criticizes something for being genuinely empty of substance or interest -- contrast it with puerile, taught earlier in this unit, which criticizes something specifically for being childish rather than simply dull.
